data.motivation: The forward map theta -> u(x_s,t_j) is smooth (explicit FD with stable step), the Fisher condition number is moderate (~62), and CRB relative std is 0.5–2% per parameter, so the problem is locally well-conditioned. The remaining failure modes of LM are (i) poor starts in the corners of the box (k1,k4 weakly determined, near-flat directions) and (ii) bias of the mode under the bounded uniform prior when the likelihood is truncated by the box. A learned initializer addresses (i); MMSE by Laplace importance sampling addresses (ii), and MMSE is the rel_l2-optimal estimator in expectation under the true prior. Log transform equalises the scale-invariant sensitivity since the PDE's time scale goes like 1/k.
assumptions: Forward model in context equals the data-generating simulator (same 40-point grid, 200 steps, sensors [5,15,25,35]).
The least-squares landscape is locally unimodal around the learned initial guess (supported by moderate Fisher condition number, not proven).
Gaussian noise sigma=0.001 is exact and i.i.d., so Gauss–Newton Laplace approximation is reasonable.
Forward-evaluation budget suffices for 750 val samples x ~15 iterations within 120 s per experiment.

evidence.claim: CRB rel_l2 floor ~0.0185, condition number median 62.3: locally well-posed, success threshold 0.05 is ~2.7x the floor.
Prior run conjectured that bounded log-space MLE should land near the CRB floor; this hypothesis is the stronger hybrid version and remains unconfirmed.
Multistart MLE sufficiency was critiqued in a prior run, suggesting that start quality matters; hybrid init addresses that critique.

data.author: researcher-experimental
data.title: MMSE readout beats the MLE mode at the box edges: learned init + LM refinement with posterior-mean estimator
data.hypothesis: A hybrid estimator will reach val rel_l2 below the 0.0193 achieved by bounded log-space MLE in a prior run. It uses an extra-trees initializer, followed by log-space LM refinement through the forward model, and reads out the posterior mean (importance sampling on the Laplace approximation under the uniform box prior) instead of the mode. The gain should come mostly from k1 and k4. Those are the least-determined parameters (CRB rel std about 0.02). Near the box bounds, the mode is pinned or truncated, while the box-truncated posterior mean shrinks error under squared loss.
data.motivation: The metric is a squared-error-type loss (rel_l2), so the Bayes-optimal point estimate is the posterior mean, not the mode. The noise is small (sigma=0.001) and the Fisher condition number is moderate (about 62), so the posterior is close to Gaussian in the interior. In that region, mode and mean should agree and both sit near the CRB floor of about 0.0185. The prior is uniform on [0.5, 2], so a non-trivial fraction of draws have k1 or k4 within a few posterior standard deviations of a bound. There the Gaussian posterior is truncated, and the MMSE estimate can beat the MLE because it is biased toward the interior. This is a measurement-limited regime where the estimator choice, not the model class, should be the remaining lever. The learned init exists to cut LM iterations so the run fits the 400 worker-second budget, and to avoid any spurious local minima.
assumptions: The harness forward model is the same explicit FD simulator (40 points, 200 steps) that generated the data, so there is no model-form error.
The noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with known sigma=0.001, so the Gauss-Newton Laplace approximation is a reasonable importance-sampling proposal.
The val split draws k from the stated i.i.d. uniform prior, so the box-truncation effect is present at the expected frequency.
The extra-trees initializer lands within the LM basin of attraction, with initializer error well below 0.1 rel_l2.
The posterior is unimodal at this noise level. If it is not, Laplace-based importance sampling underestimates the MMSE benefit.

evidence.claim: Bounded log-space MLE through the forward model already reached val rel_l2 0.0193, close to the CRB floor estimate of 0.0185, which indicates a noise-limited regime.
The CRB relative std is 0.0215 for k1 and 0.0174 for k4, versus about 0.005 for k2 and k3. Most of the error budget therefore sits in the edge segments, where any estimator improvement must show up.

In a correctly specified Gaussian-error model, the Bayes estimator is asymptotically efficient. Asymptotically, then, MMSE should match the MLE efficiency rather than lose to it, and any gain must come from finite-sample or boundary effects.

Asymptotically, the squared-error Bayes estimate and an efficient point estimate coincide to first order. If the boundary effect is negligible, MMSE and MLE should be statistically indistinguishable, which is a real risk to this hypothesis.
The CRB floor of 0.0185 is a bound for unbiased estimators only. Biased, prior-aware estimators can go below it near the support boundary.

citations.note: Several of its assumptions hold here. The explicit FD scheme is a finite-dimensional ODE/difference model, the regression model is correctly specified because we use the same simulator, and the errors are Gaussian. Its asymptotic regime (n going to infinity) does not strictly hold, since we have a fixed set of about 800 readings per sample. The result supports near-efficiency of the Bayes estimate, not superiority over the MLE.

It is a statement about the squared-error Bayes estimate in an i.i.d.-sample Hellinger/nonparametric setting with a prior that has a finite first moment. The uniform box prior satisfies the moment condition. Our observations are not i.i.d. replicates of one distribution, and the theorem is asymptotic. It only says that the mean and an efficient estimator agree to first order, so the predicted gain is a finite-sample boundary effect that this theorem does not cover.

data.falsifiable_test: Compare val rel_l2 of this hybrid (posterior_mean) against the prior-run MLE value of 0.0193. If budget allows, also compare against the same hybrid with estimator=mode. Additionally, stratify per-parameter error by whether the true k1 or k4 lies within 0.1 of a bound. import numpy as np
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPRegressor
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

class M:
    def fit(self, X, y):
        c = self.c
        rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
        X = np.asarray(X, float).reshape(len(X), -1)
        y = np.asarray(y, float)
        lo = np.asarray(c.lower, float)
        hi = np.asarray(c.upper, float)
        n = int(self.p.get('n_extra', 6000))
        Xa, ya = X, y
        try:
            th = lo + (hi - lo) * rng.random((n, len(lo)))
            F = np.asarray(c.forward(th), float).reshape(n, -1)
            if F.shape[1] == X.shape[1]:
                Xs = F + c.noise_std * rng.standard_normal(F.shape)
                Xa = np.vstack([X, Xs])
                ya = np.vstack([y, th])
        except Exception:
            pass
        self.sx = StandardScaler().fit(Xa)
        self.my = ya.mean(0)
        self.sy = ya.std(0) + 1e-12
        self.m = MLPRegressor(hidden_layer_sizes=(256, 256), alpha=1e-5, learning_rate_init=1e-3, max_iter=200, early_stopping=True, n_iter_no_change=15, random_state=0)
        self.m.fit(self.sx.transform(Xa), (ya - self.my) / self.sy)
        return self
    def predict(self, X):
        X = np.asarray(X, float).reshape(len(X), -1)
        out = self.m.predict(self.sx.transform(X)) * self.sy + self.my
        return self.c.clip(out)

def build_method(params, context):
    m = M()
    m.p = params
    m.c = context
    return m

method.code:
import numpy as np
import torch

class M:
    def __init__(s, p, c):
        s.p = p; s.c = c; s.ok = False; s.resid = -1.0
    def fit(s, X, y):
        X = np.asarray(X, float); y = np.asarray(y, float); c = s.c
        lo = np.asarray(c.lower, float); hi = np.asarray(c.upper, float)
        s.lo, s.hi = lo, hi
        rng = np.random.default_rng(0); sig = float(c.noise_std)
        clean = []; th_s = []
        try:
            F = np.asarray(c.forward(y[:64]), float).reshape(64, -1)
            if F.shape[1] == X.shape[1]:
                s.resid = float(np.std(F - X[:64]))
                s.ok = s.resid < 5 * sig
        except Exception:
            s.ok = False
        if s.ok:
            n = int(s.p.get('n_extra', 12000))
            for i in range(0, n, 2000):
                th = rng.uniform(lo, hi, size=(2000, len(lo)))
                try:
                    F = np.asarray(c.forward(th), float).reshape(2000, -1)
                except Exception:
                    break
                clean.append(F); th_s.append(th)
        Xc = np.vstack(clean) if clean else np.zeros((0, X.shape[1]))
        yc = np.vstack(th_s) if th_s else np.zeros((0, y.shape[1]))
        Xall = np.vstack([X, Xc + sig * rng.standard_normal(Xc.shape)])
        yl = np.log(np.vstack([y, yc]))
        s.mu = Xall.mean(0); s.sd = Xall.std(0) + 1e-8
        s.ym = yl.mean(0); s.ys = yl.std(0) + 1e-8
        d = X.shape[1]; torch.manual_seed(0)
        s.net = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(d, 512), torch.nn.GELU(), torch.nn.Linear(512, 256), torch.nn.GELU(), torch.nn.Linear(256, 128), torch.nn.GELU(), torch.nn.Linear(128, y.shape[1]))
        ep = int(s.p.get('epochs', 60)); bs = int(s.p.get('batch', 256))
        opt = torch.optim.AdamW(s.net.parameters(), lr=float(s.p.get('lr', 1e-3)), weight_decay=1e-4)
        sch = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(opt, T_max=ep)
        Yt = torch.tensor((yl - s.ym) / s.ys, dtype=torch.float32)
        for e in range(ep):
            Xe = np.vstack([X, Xc + sig * rng.standard_normal(Xc.shape)])
            Xt = torch.tensor((Xe - s.mu) / s.sd, dtype=torch.float32)
            perm = torch.randperm(Xt.shape[0])
            for j in range(0, Xt.shape[0], bs):
                idx = perm[j:j + bs]
                opt.zero_grad()
                loss = ((s.net(Xt[idx]) - Yt[idx]) ** 2).mean()
                loss.backward(); opt.step()
            sch.step()
        return s
    def predict(s, X):
        X = np.asarray(X, float)
        with torch.no_grad():
            o = s.net(torch.tensor((X - s.mu) / s.sd, dtype=torch.float32)).numpy()
        return np.clip(np.exp(o * s.ys + s.ym), s.lo, s.hi)

def build_method(params, context):
    return M(params, context)

data.title: Learning-curve point n≈9000 with P-013's recipe: is the amortised-network gap to the CRB floor sample-limited?
data.hypothesis: With P-013's architecture and loss held fixed, adding 6000 fresh prior-predictive simulations (with per-epoch resampled sigma=0.001 noise) reduces val rel_l2 to < 0.0225. The excess MSE over the physics floor (P-014) shrinks by at least 30% relative to P-013 (n=3000).
data.motivation: The pilots show the physics estimator sits at the CRB floor, about 0.0184. Any amortised-network gap is therefore approximation or estimation error of the map y -> E[k|y]. For a fixed function class, estimation error decays with n (roughly n^-1 for a parametric-rate excess risk). A capacity or optimisation floor would instead be flat in n. A 9k point between P-013 (3k) and P-011 (15k, same code) gives a 3-point curve and separates these two cases. The cost is low because forwards are cheap and inference needs no forward calls. This matters practically: if the gap closes, an amortised estimator can replace per-sample LM at test time.
assumptions: context.forward(theta) returns noise-free observations in the same flattened layout as the training features. The code checks the shapes and falls back to the given data only if they differ.
The forward budget allows 6000 extra evaluations (the pilot used about 14k in seconds).

P-013's torch_mlp internals (LayerNorm+GELU, AdamW, cosine) are reproduced closely enough. Remaining implementation differences, such as early-stopping details, are second-order compared with a 3x change in n.
The harness rel_l2 is a vector-norm relative error. Excess is therefore measured in MSE on the metric's own scale, not against per-parameter CRB values.

evidence.claim: Forward consistency: residual std at truth 0.00099 vs 0.001, no mismatch over 200 samples, so simulated draws follow the data law.
The physics and hybrid pilots both reach about 0.0184. The noise floor for any posterior-mean estimator is therefore near that value.
The posterior is locally near-Gaussian (z_rms 1.00, chi2/dof 0.94), so E[k|y] is a smooth function of y. That favours a parametric-like learning rate.
Seed variance (about 0.001-0.002) may be comparable to the effect, so a single-seed 9k point can be inconclusive.
Per-epoch noise resampling is stronger augmentation than P-013's noise_aug=2, so P-013 vs this arm confounds n with augmentation.

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class M:
    def fit(self, X, y):
        c = self.c
        p = self.p
        rng = np.random.default_rng(int(p.get('seed', 0)))
        torch.manual_seed(int(p.get('seed', 0)))
        X = np.asarray(X, float).reshape(len(X), -1)
        y = np.asarray(y, float)
        lo = np.asarray(c.lower, float)
        hi = np.asarray(c.upper, float)
        n = int(p.get('n_extra', 6000))
        s = float(c.noise_std)
        F = None
        th = None
        try:
            th = lo + (hi - lo) * rng.random((n, len(lo)))
            F0 = np.asarray(c.forward(th), float).reshape(n, -1)
            if F0.shape[1] == X.shape[1] and np.all(np.isfinite(F0)):
                F = F0
        except Exception:
            F = None
        if F is not None:
            nh = max(1, n // 20)
            Fh, thh = F[:nh] + s * rng.standard_normal(F[:nh].shape), th[:nh]
            Ft, tht = F[nh:], th[nh:]
            Xref = np.vstack([X, Ft + s * rng.standard_normal(Ft.shape)])
        else:
            nh = max(1, len(X) // 20)
            Fh, thh = X[:nh], y[:nh]
            Ft, tht = None, None
            X, y = X[nh:], y[nh:]
            Xref = X
        self.mx = Xref.mean(0)
        self.sx = Xref.std(0) + 1e-8
        ly = np.log(np.vstack([y, tht]) if tht is not None else y)
        self.my = ly.mean(0)
        self.sy = ly.std(0) + 1e-8
        d = X.shape[1]
        net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 512), nn.LayerNorm(512), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(512, 256), nn.LayerNorm(256), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(256, 128), nn.LayerNorm(128), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(128, y.shape[1]))
        E = int(p.get('epochs', 60))
        opt = torch.optim.AdamW(net.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4)
        sch = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(opt, max(1, E))
        Xh = torch.tensor((Fh - self.mx) / self.sx, dtype=torch.float32)
        Yh = torch.tensor((np.log(thh) - self.my) / self.sy, dtype=torch.float32)
        Zg = (np.log(y) - self.my) / self.sy
        Zs = (np.log(tht) - self.my) / self.sy if tht is not None else None
        best = 1e30
        state = None
        for ep in range(E):
            if Ft is not None:
                Xe = np.vstack([X, Ft + s * rng.standard_normal(Ft.shape)])
                Ye = np.vstack([Zg, Zs])
            else:
                Xe, Ye = X, Zg
            Xt = torch.tensor((Xe - self.mx) / self.sx, dtype=torch.float32)
            Yt = torch.tensor(Ye, dtype=torch.float32)
            net.train()
            perm = torch.randperm(len(Xt))
            for i in range(0, len(Xt), 128):
                b = perm[i:i + 128]
                opt.zero_grad()
                loss = ((net(Xt[b]) - Yt[b]) ** 2).mean()
                loss.backward()
                opt.step()
            sch.step()
            net.eval()
            with torch.no_grad():
                v = float(((net(Xh) - Yh) ** 2).mean())
            if v < best:
                best = v
                state = {k: t.clone() for k, t in net.state_dict().items()}
        if state is not None:
            net.load_state_dict(state)
        net.eval()
        self.net = net
        return self
    def predict(self, X):
        X = np.asarray(X, float).reshape(len(X), -1)
        with torch.no_grad():
            z = self.net(torch.tensor((X - self.mx) / self.sx, dtype=torch.float32)).numpy()
        return self.c.clip(np.exp(z * self.sy + self.my))

def build_method(params, context):
    m = M()
    m.p = params
    m.c = context
    return m

feasibility.notes: 6000 forward evals take a few seconds. Torch 512-256-128 on 9000 rows x d features for 60 epochs is about 70 batches per epoch, roughly 15-35 s on CPU. No forward calls at predict time. Falls back to given-data training if the forward output layout mismatches.

import numpy as np
import torch

class M:
    def __init__(s, p, c):
        s.p = p; s.c = c; s.ok = False; s.resid = -1.0; s.n_sim = 0
    def fit(s, X, y):
        X = np.asarray(X, float); y = np.asarray(y, float); c = s.c
        lo = np.asarray(c.lower, float); hi = np.asarray(c.upper, float)
        s.lo, s.hi = lo, hi
        rng = np.random.default_rng(0); sig = float(c.noise_std)
        d = X.shape[1]; q = y.shape[1]
        Xc = np.zeros((0, d)); yc = np.ones((0, q))
        try:
            F = np.asarray(c.forward(y[:64]), float).reshape(64, -1)
            if F.shape[1] == d:
                s.resid = float(np.std(F - X[:64])); s.ok = s.resid < 5 * sig
        except Exception:
            s.ok = False
        if s.ok:
            n = int(s.p.get('n_extra', 12000)); A = []; B = []
            for i in range(0, n, 2000):
                th = rng.uniform(lo, hi, size=(2000, q))
                try:
                    A.append(np.asarray(c.forward(th), float).reshape(2000, -1)); B.append(th)
                except Exception:
                    break
            if A:
                Xc = np.vstack(A); yc = np.vstack(B)
        s.n_sim = len(Xc)
        s.mu = X.mean(0); s.sd = X.std(0) + 1e-8
        yl = np.log(y); s.ym = yl.mean(0); s.ys = yl.std(0) + 1e-8
        perm = rng.permutation(len(X)); nh = max(1, len(X) // 10)
        ih = perm[:nh]; it = perm[nh:]
        T = lambda a: torch.tensor(np.asarray(a), dtype=torch.float32)
        Xo = T((X[it] - s.mu) / s.sd); Yo = T((yl[it] - s.ym) / s.ys)
        Xh = T((X[ih] - s.mu) / s.sd); Yh = T((yl[ih] - s.ym) / s.ys)
        Xs = T(Xc); Ys = T((np.log(yc) - s.ym) / s.ys)
        mu = T(s.mu); sd = T(s.sd)
        torch.manual_seed(0)
        nn = torch.nn
        s.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 256), nn.LayerNorm(256), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.LayerNorm(256), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(256, q))
        ep = int(s.p.get('epochs', 60)); bs = int(s.p.get('batch', 256))
        opt = torch.optim.AdamW(s.net.parameters(), lr=float(s.p.get('lr', 1e-3)), weight_decay=float(s.p.get('wd', 1e-4)))
        sch = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(opt, T_max=ep)
        best = 1e30; bst = None
        for e in range(ep):
            s.net.train()
            if len(Xs) > 0:
                Xn = (Xs + sig * torch.randn_like(Xs) - mu) / sd
                Xa = torch.cat([Xo, Xn]); Ya = torch.cat([Yo, Ys])
            else:
                Xa = Xo; Ya = Yo
            idx = torch.randperm(len(Xa))
            for j in range(0, len(Xa), bs):
                b = idx[j:j + bs]
                opt.zero_grad()
                l = ((s.net(Xa[b]) - Ya[b]) ** 2).mean()
                l.backward(); opt.step()
            sch.step()
            s.net.eval()
            with torch.no_grad():
                v = float(((s.net(Xh) - Yh) ** 2).mean())
            if v < best:
                best = v; bst = {k: t.clone() for k, t in s.net.state_dict().items()}
        if bst is not None:
            s.net.load_state_dict(bst)
        s.net.eval()
        return s
    def predict(s, X):
        X = np.asarray(X, float)
        with torch.no_grad():
            o = s.net(torch.tensor((X - s.mu) / s.sd, dtype=torch.float32)).numpy()
        k = np.exp(o * s.ys + s.ym)
        return np.clip(k, s.lo, s.hi)

def build_method(params, context):

data.hypothesis: Without any training data, per-sample bounded LM in log-k (3 starts, 25 iterations) with a box-truncated Laplace-IS posterior mean reaches val rel_l2 < 0.0225 on all 750 val samples (refutation threshold), and in fact < 0.020 (near-floor diagnostic). The log-k misfit is effectively unimodal on [0.5,2]^4. At most 2% of samples have chi2/dof (dof = N-4) > 1.5. At most 2% have a later start that reaches a distinct estimate (max|delta log k| > 1e-3) with a chi2 at least 1 unit lower than start 1.

data.title: Paired readout contrast: MLE (mode) vs box-truncated posterior mean, identical LM, stratified by lower/upper edge
data.label: physics-MLE[log,ms=3,it=25]
data.hypothesis: With the LM configuration identical to P-014, the mode readout has an aggregate val rel_l2 0.5-2% higher than the posterior mean. The gain is significant in the edge strata (any k_j within 2 per-sample CRB-std of 0.5 or 2.0, mostly k1/k4), and larger at the upper edge, where posteriors are wider in absolute terms. In the interior stratum the paired 95% bootstrap CI of the squared-error difference contains 0.

data.title: IS readout accuracy control: same LM, posterior_samples 512 vs 128, paired with P-014
data.label: physics-MMSE[log,ms=3,it=25]
data.hypothesis: At 128 importance samples, the posterior-mean readout's Monte Carlo error is negligible relative to the posterior width. Re-running P-014 with 512 samples changes aggregate val rel_l2 by less than 1% relative, the paired interior CI contains 0, and the per-sample estimate shift stays below 0.1 posterior std for 95% of samples. If instead the low-ESS tail (5th-percentile ESS < 20 at 128 samples) shows larger shifts, concentrated in edge samples, then the 128-sample readout is noisy exactly where the MMSE gain is supposed to live.
